summary: Specifies rules for translating YANG data models into the Document Schema Definition Languages (DSDL), a family of XML schema languages, so NETCONF content can be validated. The target languages include RELAX NG and Schematron. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: NETCONF moves configuration data around as XML, and YANG is the language that describes what that data may contain. But YANG on its own does not give you a way to check an XML document with the validation tools that already exist. This document supplies the missing link: a set of rules for turning a YANG module into standard XML schemas that a validator can run.

questions: what is yang to dsdl mapping
subtitle: Rules for turning YANG data models into standard XML schemas so NETCONF data can be checked automatically.

tldr.problem: NETCONF carries its data as XML and YANG describes that data, but YANG alone gave no standard way to check XML documents with off-the-shelf validators.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC maps YANG modules in two steps: first to a single annotated RELAX NG hybrid schema, then to a coordinated set of RELAX NG, Schematron and DSRL schemas for one chosen kind of document.
tldr.outcome: Validators can check grammar and data types, fill in defaults, and then check semantic constraints. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 7952.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The NETCONF Working Group has completed a base protocol used for configuration management. That base specification defines protocol bindings and an XML container syntax for configuration and management operations, but does not include a data modeling language or rules for how to model the configuration and state information carried by NETCONF.

The NETMOD Working Group was chartered to design a modeling language defining the semantics of operational data, configuration data, event notifications and operations, with a focus on human-friendliness. The result is the YANG data modeling language, which now serves for the normative description of NETCONF data models.

Since NETCONF uses XML for encoding its messages, it is natural to express the constraints on NETCONF content using standard XML schema languages. For this purpose the NETMOD Working Group selected the Document Schema Definition Languages being standardized as ISO/IEC 19757. The DSDL framework comprises a set of XML schema languages that address grammar rules, semantic constraints and other data modeling aspects, and do it in a coordinated and consistent way. The three parts that the mapping relies on, RELAX NG, Schematron and DSRL, already have the status of an ISO/IEC International Standard and are supported in a number of software tools.

This document contains a specification of a mapping that translates YANG data models to XML schemas using a subset of the DSDL schema languages. The mapping is divided into two steps. In the first step, the structure of the data tree, the signatures of remote procedure call operations and notifications are expressed as the so-called hybrid schema, a single RELAX NG schema with annotations representing additional data model information such as metadata, documentation, semantic constraints and default values. The second step then generates a coordinated set of DSDL schemas that can be used for validating specific XML documents such as client requests, server responses or notifications, perhaps also taking into account additional context such as active capabilities or features.
sections.plainLanguage: NETCONF moves configuration data around as XML, and YANG is the language that describes what that data may contain. But YANG on its own does not give you a way to check an XML document with the validation tools that already exist. This document supplies the missing link: a set of rules for turning a YANG module into standard XML schemas that a validator can run.

sections.title: Objectives and Motivation
sections.content:
The main objective of this work is to complement YANG as a data modeling language with the validation capabilities of the DSDL schema languages, RELAX NG, Schematron and DSRL. The document describes the correspondence between grammatical, semantic and data type constraints expressed in YANG and equivalent DSDL patterns and rules. The ultimate goal is to be able to capture all substantial information contained in YANG modules and express it in DSDL schemas. While the mapping from YANG to DSDL may in principle be invertible, the inverse mapping from DSDL to YANG is beyond the scope of the document.

XML-based information models and XML-encoded data appear in several different forms during YANG data modelling and the NETCONF workflow: configuration datastore contents, RPC requests and replies, and notifications. RPC operations are characterized by an inherent diversity resulting from the selective availability of capabilities and features, and YANG modules can also define new RPC operations. The mapping should accommodate this variability and generate schemas that are tailored to a particular situation, and thus considerably more effective for validation than generic all-encompassing schemas.

To cope with this variability, the document assumes that the DSDL schemas will be generated on demand for a particular purpose from the available collection of YANG modules, and that their lifetime will be relatively short. It does not envision that any collection of DSDL schemas will be created and maintained over an extended period of time in parallel to YANG modules.

The generated schemas are primarily intended as input to existing XML schema validators and other off-the-shelf tools. They may also be read by developers and users as a formal representation of the constraints on a particular XML-encoded data object, so a secondary goal is to keep the schemas as readable as possible. To that end the complexity of the mapping is distributed into two steps: the first maps one or more YANG modules to the hybrid schema, a single RELAX NG schema describing the grammatical constraints for the main data tree as well as for RPC operations and notifications, with semantic constraints and other information recorded as foreign namespace annotations; the second transforms the hybrid schema into a coordinated set of fully conformant DSDL schemas containing the constraints for a particular data object and a specific situation, intended mainly for machine validation.
sections.plainLanguage: The aim is to carry over everything a YANG module says into a form a validator understands, so that a document can be checked against the model it claims to follow. Because RPCs and notifications come in many shapes, the schemas are made to order for one kind of document rather than one giant schema that covers everything. Keeping the schemas readable matters too, because people read them.

sections.title: The Three DSDL Schema Languages
sections.content:
Document Schema Definition Languages is a framework of schema languages being developed as the International Standard ISO/IEC 19757. Unlike other approaches to XML document validation, most notably W3C XML Schema Definition, the DSDL framework adheres to the principle of small languages: each constituent is a stand-alone schema language with a relatively narrow purpose and focus. Together these languages may be used in a coordinated way to accomplish various validation tasks. The mapping uses three of them.

RELAX NG is an XML schema language for grammar-based validation. Like XSD it can describe constraints on the structure and contents of XML documents, but unlike the DTD and XSD schema languages it intentionally avoids any infoset augmentation such as defining default values. In the DSDL architecture that task is delegated to DSRL. As its base data type library, RELAX NG uses the W3C XML Schema Datatypes, but other data type libraries may be used alongside it or replace it. RELAX NG is very liberal in accepting annotations from other namespaces, which is what the mapping relies on. It has an XML syntax and a compact syntax, and the mapping specification uses exclusively the XML syntax, though the resulting schemas may be presented in the equivalent compact syntax.

Schematron is Part 3 of DSDL and reached the status of a full ISO/IEC standard in 2006. In contrast to the traditional schema languages based on the concept of a formal grammar, Schematron uses a rule-based approach, and its rules may specify arbitrary conditions involving data from different parts of an XML document. Each rule consists of three components: a context, which is an XPath expression defining the set of locations where the rule is to be applied; an assert or report condition, another XPath expression evaluated relative to the location matched by the context expression; and a human-readable message displayed when the assert condition is false or the report condition is true. The difference between the two conditions is that the assert is positive, stating a condition that a valid document has to satisfy, whereas the report specifies an error condition.

DSRL is Part 8 of DSDL and reached the status of a full ISO/IEC standard in 2008. Unlike RELAX NG and Schematron, DSRL is allowed to modify the XML information set of the validated document. While primarily intended for renaming XML elements and attributes, it can also define default values for XML attributes and default contents for XML elements or subtrees, so that the default contents are inserted if they are missing in the validated documents. That last feature is what the mapping uses to represent YANG default contents consisting of leaf nodes with default values and their ancestor non-presence containers.
sections.plainLanguage: The DSDL family is a set of small, single-purpose schema languages meant to be used together. RELAX NG checks the shape of the document and the types of its values. Schematron checks rules that can look at several parts of the document at once, and it can produce a message for a person to read. DSRL is the one that is allowed to change the document, which is how default values get filled in.

sections.title: Overview of the Mapping
sections.content:
The mapping procedure is divided into two steps. The transformation T in the first step maps one or more YANG modules to the hybrid schema. Constraints that cannot be expressed directly in RELAX NG, such as list key definitions and must statements, and various documentation texts are recorded in the schema as foreign-namespace annotations. In the second step, the hybrid schema may be transformed in multiple ways to a coordinated set of DSDL schemas that can be used for validating a particular data object in a specific context. Appropriate parts of the hybrid schema are extracted and specific annotations transformed to equivalent, but usually more complex, Schematron patterns and DSRL element maps.

An implementation of the mapping algorithm MUST accept one or more valid YANG modules as its input. It is important to be able to process multiple YANG modules together, since multiple modules may be negotiated for a NETCONF session and the contents of the configuration datastore is then obtained as the union of the data trees specified by the individual modules, which may also lead to multiple root nodes of the datastore hierarchy. The input modules may be further coupled by the augment statement, in which one module augments the data tree of another. It is also assumed that the algorithm has access, perhaps on demand, to all the YANG modules that the input modules import, directly or transitively.

Other information contained in the input YANG modules, such as semantic constraints and default values, is recorded in the hybrid schema as annotations qualified with the namespace URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netmod:dsdl-annotations:1. Metadata describing the YANG modules is mapped to Dublin Core annotation elements, and documentation strings are mapped to documentation elements belonging to the DTD compatibility vocabulary.

The output of the second step is a coordinated set of three DSDL schemas corresponding to a specific data object and context: a RELAX NG schema describing the grammatical and data type constraints; a Schematron schema expressing other constraints such as the uniqueness of list keys or user-specified semantic rules; and a DSRL schema containing the specification of default contents.
sections.plainLanguage: First the YANG modules become one annotated RELAX NG file, the hybrid schema, which holds everything the modules said, including the things RELAX NG cannot express. Then that file is cut up and rewritten into a set of schemas for one particular kind of document: a RELAX NG schema for the shape, a Schematron schema for the rules, and a DSRL schema for the defaults.

sections.title: NETCONF Content Validation
sections.content: The schemas generated by the mapping are applied to validate XML instance documents such as the contents of a datastore or various NETCONF messages. The validation proceeds in three steps. First, the XML instance document is checked for grammatical and data type validity using the RELAX NG schema. Second, default values for leaf nodes have to be applied and their ancestor containers added where necessary. It is important to add the implicit nodes before the next validation step, because the YANG specification requires that the data tree against which XPath expressions are evaluated already has all defaults filled in, and this step modifies the information set of the validated XML document. Third, the semantic constraints are checked using the Schematron schema.
sections.plainLanguage: Validating an XML document takes three passes. The first checks that the structure and the value types are right. The second fills in the default values and adds the containers that hold them, so that the third pass sees a complete tree. The third pass then checks the rules that span the document.

sections.title: The Hybrid Schema
sections.content:
The first step of the mapping produces an intermediate document, the hybrid schema, which specifies all the constraints for the entire data model using the RELAX NG syntax and additional annotations. It cannot be directly used for validation: as a matter of fact it is not even a valid RELAX NG schema, because it contains multiple schemas demarcated by special annotation elements. Every input YANG module corresponds to exactly one embedded grammar in the hybrid schema, and that separation allows each embedded grammar to include named pattern definitions into its own namespace, which is important for mapping YANG groupings.

YANG modules provide other important information that cannot be expressed in a RELAX NG schema: semantic constraints, default values, metadata, documentation and so on. Such items are represented in the hybrid schema as XML attributes and elements belonging to the namespace with the URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netmod:dsdl-annotations:1. In most cases the annotation attributes and elements have the same name as the corresponding YANG statement.

YANG modules define data models not only for configuration and state data but also for RPC operations and event notifications. To capture all three types of data model in one schema document, the hybrid schema uses special markers that enclose sub-schemas for configuration and state data, for the RPC operations with their input and output parts, and for the individual notifications. The markers are the elements nma:data, nma:rpcs, nma:rpc, nma:input, nma:output, nma:notifications and nma:notification, all in the NETMOD-specific annotation namespace.

Besides the DSDL schema languages, the mapping also uses three sets of annotations added as foreign-namespace attributes and elements to RELAX NG schemas. Two of them, Dublin Core elements and DTD compatibility annotations, are standard vocabularies for representing metadata and documentation respectively. Although these items are not used for formal validation, they often carry important information for data model implementers, so they SHOULD be included in the hybrid schema and MAY also appear in the final validation schemas. The third set, the NETMOD-specific annotations, conveys semantic constraints and other information that cannot be expressed directly in RELAX NG, and in the second mapping step these annotations are converted to Schematron and DSRL rules.
sections.plainLanguage: The hybrid schema is the intermediate file, and it is deliberately not a usable schema on its own: it holds several RELAX NG grammars in one document, so it cannot be handed to a validator. One grammar is produced for each YANG module, which keeps the pattern names of one module from colliding with another's. Anything RELAX NG cannot say, such as list keys, must statements, defaults and documentation, is attached to the grammar as annotations.

sections.title: Mapping the Hybrid Schema to DSDL
sections.content:
The second mapping step takes the hybrid schema and transforms it into various DSDL schemas capable of validating instance XML documents. As an input parameter, it takes, in the simplest case, just a specification of the NETCONF XML document type that is to be validated: the contents of a datastore, a reply to a get or get-config operation, the contents of other RPC requests and replies, and event notifications.

The second mapping step has three general tasks. First, it extracts the parts of the hybrid schema that are appropriate for the requested document type: if a get reply is to be validated, the subtree under the data marker has to be selected. Second, the schema must be adapted to the specific encapsulating XML elements mandated by the RPC layer, for example the rpc and data elements in the case of a get reply, or the notification element for a notification. Third, the NETMOD-specific annotations that are relevant for the schema language of the generated schema must be mapped to the corresponding patterns or rules. These three tasks are together much simpler than the first mapping step and can be effectively implemented using XSL transformations.

Obtaining a validating RELAX NG schema from the hybrid schema only means taking the appropriate parts and assembling them in a new grammar, perhaps after removing unwanted annotations. Global named pattern definitions must be moved to a separate schema file, and patterns defining the top-level information items of the target document type must be added. To avoid copying common definitions for common NETCONF elements into every output file, such schema-independent definitions should be collected in a library file that is then included by the validating RELAX NG schemas.

Schematron schemas are flatter and more uniform than RELAX NG ones, with exactly four levels of XML hierarchy: schema, pattern, rule, and assert or report. The semantic annotations in the hybrid schema, which are the must, key, unique, max-elements, min-elements, when, leafref and leaf-list annotations, are mapped to corresponding Schematron rules, as is the mandatory attribute appearing on a choice. Each input YANG module is mapped to a Schematron pattern whose id attribute is set to the module name, and every element pattern containing one of those annotations becomes a Schematron rule whose context attribute holds the absolute path of the context element in the data tree.

The document also requests two IETF XML namespace registrations: urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netmod:dsdl-annotations:1 for the NETMOD-specific annotations, and urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netmod:xpath-extensions:1 for the NETMOD-specific XPath extension functions.
sections.plainLanguage: The second step is mostly cutting and rewriting. It picks out the part of the hybrid schema that matches the document being checked, wraps it in the XML elements the NETCONF layer requires, and turns the leftover annotations into real Schematron rules or DSRL rules. The RFC says this step is simple enough to implement with XSLT.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document defines a procedure that maps data models expressed in the YANG language to a coordinated set of DSDL schemas. The procedure itself has no security impact on the Internet.

DSDL schemas obtained by the mapping procedure may be used for validating the contents of NETCONF messages or entire datastores, and thus they provide additional validity checks above those performed by NETCONF server and client implementations supporting YANG data models. The strictness of this validation is directly derived from the source YANG modules that the validated XML data adhere to.
sections.plainLanguage: The mapping itself has no security effect. What it produces does: the schemas give a NETCONF client or server a way to check that data matches its model, which is an extra check on top of the ones the protocol already does. How strict that check is depends entirely on how strict the YANG module was written.

items.title: Step 1: grammar
items.text: Check the document against the RELAX NG schema for grammar and data type validity.

items.title: Step 2: defaults
items.text: Fill in default values for leaf nodes and add the ancestor containers that hold them.

items.title: Step 3: semantics
items.text: Check the semantic constraints with the Schematron schema, on the tree with defaults already applied.

viz.caption: THE SHAPE OF A HYBRID SCHEMA (RFC 6110, SECTION 8.1)

data.title: Hybrid schema for one YANG module
data.code:
<grammar xmlns="http://relaxng.org/ns/structure/1.0"
         xmlns:nma="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netmod:dsdl-annotations:1"
         xmlns:exa="http://example.com/ns/example-a">
  <start>
    <grammar nma:module="example-a"
             ns="http://example.com/ns/example-a">
      <start>
        <nma:data>
          ...configuration and state data defined in "example-a"...
        </nma:data>
        <nma:rpcs>
          <nma:rpc>
            <nma:input>
              <element name="exa:myrpc"> ... </element>
            </nma:input>
            <nma:output> ... </nma:output>
          </nma:rpc>
        </nma:rpcs>
        <nma:notifications>
          <nma:notification>
            <element name="exa:mynotif"> ... </element>
          </nma:notification>
        </nma:notifications>
      </start>
    </grammar>
  </start>
</grammar>
